topics.title: News Feed
topics.concepts: Fan-out on write/read, ranking, caching, pagination
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a social news feed (like Facebook, X or LinkedIn): users post, follow others, and see a ranked, reasonably fresh feed of posts from people they follow, at a scale where some accounts have millions of followers. The classic discussion is **fan-out on write vs. fan-out on read**, **ranking**, **caching** and **pagination**.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Create posts (text or media). Follow and unfollow.
- `GET /feed?cursor=` returns a ranked feed, paginated, with new posts appearing within seconds.

**Non-functional**
- Feed reads are p99 < 200 ms and read-heavy (≈ 100 reads per post).
- A celebrity posting must not cause a write storm that degrades everything.

**Scale:** 300M DAU, each opening the feed 10 times a day, is 3B feed reads/day ≈ 35k/s (peak ~100k/s). 50M posts/day ≈ 600 writes/s. Average 200 followers per user means **fan-out ≈ 120k feed inserts/s**.

## 1. Scope and selected architecture

I serve a follower feed with public/private posts, deletion and paginated reads. I choose hybrid fan-out because follower counts are skewed: precomputing one celebrity's 20 million references would monopolize write workers. Inbox records store post references, not copied bodies.

## 2. APIs and assembly algorithm

```text
POST /posts {body,visibility} -> postId
GET /feed?cursor=... -> items,nextCursor
Post PK(postId): authorId,createdAt,version,visibility,deleted
Inbox PK(userId,sortKey,postId): sourceEventId
Follow PK(followerId,authorId): state,version
```

Post creation commits with an outbox event. Fan-out workers batch idempotent inbox inserts for ordinary authors. Feed assembly merges inbox candidates with recent celebrity posts, checks current follow/privacy/deletion state, ranks eligible candidates and returns a stable tie-breaker cursor. A ranking-session snapshot or stated approximate continuation policy handles changing scores. At 100,000 inbox insertions/s, a 20-million-follower post alone needs about 200 seconds, motivating the hybrid threshold. Deletion marks authority first; stale references are filtered before later cleanup. Read latency, oldest fan-out age, candidate shortfall and hot-author load are separate signals.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![News Feed: Post service commits Post store; Post service outbox Fanout queue; Fanout queue ordinary authors Follower inbox; Follower inbox candidates Feed assembler; Celebrity post index pull candidates Feed assembler; Feed assembler authorize then rank Visibility and ranker](designs/hld-5.svg)](designs/hld-5.svg)

**Fan-out on write** distributes post references to follower inboxes. **Fan-out on read** gathers posts when the reader asks. **Ranking** orders candidates; it should not be confused with retrieving authorized candidates in the first place.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Ordinary authors and celebrity authors can use different fan-out policies.](lessons/hld-5-flow.svg)

*Ordinary authors and celebrity authors can use different fan-out policies.*

![A stored feed reference is not permanent permission to view content.](lessons/hld-5-failure.svg)

*A stored feed reference is not permanent permission to view content.*

### Calculate the fan-out trade-off

A post by someone with 500 followers creates roughly 500 inbox insertions. A celebrity with 20 million followers creates 20 million. At 100,000 insertions/s, that single fan-out takes about 200 seconds before other traffic. A hybrid avoids requiring every follower inbox to be updated before the celebrity post is visible.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Architecture

- **Post service** writes the post to a posts store (sharded by postId) and emits `PostCreated` to Kafka.
- **Fan-out service** consumes the event, reads the author's followers (graph store), and pushes `postId` into each follower's **feed cache** (a Redis list or sorted set capped at ~800 IDs).
- **Feed service** reads the user's precomputed IDs, merges in posts from followed celebrities (pull), hydrates the posts (cache plus batch get), ranks, and paginates.

### Key design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Push (fan-out on write).** Reads are fast (precomputed). The cost is write amplification: a 10M-follower account means 10M inserts per post, plus wasted work for inactive followers.

**2. Pull (fan-out on read).** No write amplification. The cost is expensive reads: merging hundreds of followees' timelines on each request.

**3. Hybrid (one possible model).** Push for normal users. Pull for accounts above a follower threshold (e.g. 100k) and merge their recent posts at read time. Also skip pushing to inactive users and rebuild their feed on next login.

**4. Ranking.** Reverse-chronological is simplest. Ranked feeds score a candidate set (precomputed IDs plus celebrity posts, a few hundred items) with features such as recency, affinity, engagement and content type. Two-stage: cheap candidate generation, then a heavier ranker on the top few hundred.

**5. Pagination.** Use **cursor-based** (last seen score or ID), not offset. New posts arriving at the top don't shift pages, and it's O(1) to resume.

**6. Storage.** Feed cache in Redis holds IDs only (small). Posts are hydrated from a post cache. The follow graph lives in a sharded store with both `followers(user)` and `following(user)` indexes.

### Scope, guarantees and sizing assumptions

**Correctness requirement:** A feed item must respect current visibility even when fanout and caches lag.

Assume 5 million daily users x 20 feed reads: 100 million/day, about 1,157 reads/s. One celebrity with 10 million followers creates 10 million fanout writes per post; average users cannot represent this tail.

### API contracts and data ownership

```text
POST /posts; GET /feed?cursor=...; POST /follow; DELETE /posts/{id}
```

```text
Logical records (outline, not complete DDL):
post(id,author_id,body_ref,visibility,version); follow(follower,followee); timeline(user_id,rank_key,post_id)

Primary access/partitioning boundary:
user_id for timelines; author_id/post_id for canonical posts and follower graph
```

### Build the architecture in stages

**Stage 3 — Partition and isolate.** Partition around user_id for timelines; author_id/post_id for canonical posts and follower graph. Track ownership with a routing epoch or a database-native partition mechanism. Move virtual buckets or copy/backfill data with a verified cutover, rather than changing a modulo divisor and assuming records move themselves. Isolate bulk/background workloads from the latency-sensitive path and test the busiest tenant independently.

### Trace the critical request

Store post durably and publish creation intent; fanout workers append references to ordinary followers; on read merge cached timeline candidates with high-fanout authors, apply visibility/deletion filters, rank and paginate with a stable cursor. Hydrate post bodies from canonical storage.

### Deep dive: the decision that changes this system

Fanout-on-write lowers read latency but amplifies writes and wastes work on inactive accounts. Fanout-on-read avoids those writes but adds merge cost. A hybrid handles celebrity skew; threshold selection must use measured follower counts and active-reader behavior.

### Failure and race-condition walkthrough

A post is deleted after fanout reaches some timelines. A canonical tombstone/version and read-time visibility check stop old references from displaying it; deleting every cached timeline synchronously is not a reliable boundary.

### Security, tenancy and lifecycle

### Trade-offs and a starting recommendation

Ranking by timestamp is predictable; learned ranking needs feature freshness, versioned models and offline/online evaluation. Cursor pagination on a changing ranked set needs snapshot/ranking epoch semantics; offset pagination causes duplicates and omissions.

Measure feed p99, fanout lag, stale visibility exposure, candidate coverage, queue backlog by author and timeline write amplification.

**Test matrix:** Celebrity burst, inactive follower population, unfollow during fanout, deleted/private posts in stale cache, delayed queue and page continuation while new posts arrive.

### Follow-up questions with answers

**What cannot be eventually consistent here?** The operation establishing this guarantee: A feed item must respect current visibility even when fanout and caches lag.

**What is the first scaling pressure to test?** Use the actual workload: Assume 5 million daily users x 20 feed reads: 100 million/day, about 1,157 reads/s. One celebrity with 10 million followers creates 10 million fanout writes per post; average users cannot represent this tail.

**Which failure would invalidate the naive design?** A post is deleted after fanout reaches some timelines. A canonical tombstone/version and read-time visibility check stop old references from displaying it; deleting every cached timeline synchronously is not a reliable boundary.

**Why not introduce every distributed component immediately?** Ranking by timestamp is predictable; learned ranking needs feature freshness, versioned models and offline/online evaluation. Cursor pagination on a changing ranked set needs snapshot/ranking epoch semantics; offset pagination causes duplicates and omissions.

**How would you demonstrate the design works?** Celebrity burst, inactive follower population, unfollow during fanout, deleted/private posts in stale cache, delayed queue and page continuation while new posts arrive. Keep the expected invariant and recovery outcome visible in the results.

### Further reading

- [PostgreSQL isolation and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html).
- [Apache Kafka delivery and transaction design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).
- [Redis rate-limiter design](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/rate-limiter/) for atomic shared-state examples.

### Work through pagination and consistency

Offset pagination can skip or duplicate posts when new items arrive. A cursor containing a stable sort key and tie-breaker gives a better continuation contract; ranking changes may require a session snapshot or an explicitly approximate feed policy.

Unfollowing should affect authorization/candidate selection even when old inbox rows remain. Store references rather than copying full post bodies into every inbox; updates and deletions then have a smaller invalidation surface. Track oldest fan-out age so an apparently healthy API does not hide stale feeds.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Does ranking decide whether private content is visible?** No. Authorization filters candidates before exposure and may need a final check.

**Must every user receive every post synchronously?** No. State the freshness promise and support delayed materialization.

## 7. Closing answer

I choose hybrid fan-out: precompute ordinary-author inbox references and fetch high-fanout authors on read. A read-time visibility check prevents stale inbox entries from leaking deleted or restricted content. Stable cursor ordering and lag metrics make freshness and pagination limitations explicit.

topics.title: RAG Fundamentals
topics.concepts: Documents + chunks + embeddings + vector DB + retrieval + LLM
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Explain Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) end to end: why it exists, the ingestion pipeline (documents → chunks → embeddings → vector store) and the query pipeline (question → retrieve → augment prompt → generate with citations), with a minimal Spring AI implementation and its typical failure modes.

## Requirements

- Why RAG instead of fine-tuning for private and changing knowledge.
- Ingestion: loading, cleaning, chunking, embedding, metadata, storage.
- Query: embedding the question, top-k retrieval, prompt assembly, grounded generation.
- Citations and "I don't know" behaviour. Failure modes and how to evaluate.

## 1. Selected RAG solution

I build a private-policy assistant without retraining weights for every policy update. Ingestion parses approved revisions, chunks meaningful sections and publishes a scoped retrieval index. At query time I authenticate, retrieve permitted candidates, select evidence within budget and ask for a cited answer. The model's general knowledge is not authoritative for the private policy.

## 2. Answer contract and execution

```text
POST /ask {question,conversationId} -> {answer,citations,abstained}
Citation: sourceId,revision,chunkId
Execution: authorize -> retrieve -> pack evidence -> generate -> validate
No supporting passage -> {answer:"No approved evidence found",abstained:true}
```

Source `leave:v3:c4` caps carry-over at five days. For “May I carry seven?”, the answer is no under that passage, citing it and identifying any unavailable exception policy. It does not invent an exception. The validator rejects citations outside retrieved authorized IDs and evaluates whether passages support claims; valid IDs alone do not prove entailment.

With 6,000 evidence tokens and 500-token chunks, fewer than twelve may fit after wrappers/metadata. I reserve output and instructions before selecting evidence. Evaluation separates source recall from supported-answer rate and includes absent answers, conflicting revisions, deleted sources and forbidden tenants. A retrieval miss is not repaired by pretending a better prompt can reconstruct private facts that were never supplied.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![RAG Fundamentals: Document ingestion publishes Versioned chunks; Versioned chunks searchable evidence Scoped retrieval; Scoped retrieval selected passages Context budgeter; Context budgeter bounded prompt ChatClient; ChatClient structured claims Citation validator; Citation validator validated result Answer or abstention](designs/ai-5.svg)](designs/ai-5.svg)

An **ingestion pipeline** prepares documents. A **retriever** selects evidence. A **grounded answer** is supported by that evidence. A **citation** points to a source; merely printing a valid source ID does not prove the source supports the sentence.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![A query uses published source versions from the retrieval index.](lessons/ai-5-flow.svg)

*A query uses published source versions from the retrieval index.*

![When the answer is absent, fluent completion is not a recovery method.](lessons/ai-5-failure.svg)

*When the answer is absent, fluent completion is not a recovery method.*

### Trace one answer

Source `leave-policy:v3:chunk4` says “Annual carry-over is capped at five days.” A question asks “Can I carry seven days?” A supported answer says no under that passage and cites it, while noting any missing exception policy. It must not invent an exception because seven sounds reasonable.

With 6,000 tokens available for evidence and chunks averaging 500 tokens, at most about 12 fit before citation wrappers and other overhead. Increasing top-k without budgeting can displace instructions or truncate important passages. Chunk boundaries should preserve meaning, not just count characters.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Mechanism and rationale

**Design question:** How can an assistant answer private-document questions without training a model on every document update?

RAG retrieves relevant authorized evidence at inference time and supplies it to a generator. Ingestion and query serving are different pipelines. Retrieval errors and generation errors must be diagnosed separately; a good model cannot cite an absent or forbidden source correctly.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Versioned source -> parse/chunk/embed -> index; question -> authorize -> retrieve/rerank -> budget context -> generate cited answer -> verify or abstain

Application contracts (design outline):
Question(tenant,user,query); Evidence(chunkId,documentVersion,passage); GroundedAnswer(text,sourceIds,abstained)
```

Use Spring AI Document, EmbeddingModel and VectorStore behind application authorization. QuestionAnswerAdvisor can provide a simple RAG path; the application still owns filtering, source versioning and answer validation.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

A 12,000-token input allowance minus 1,000 task instructions and 2,000 conversation leaves 9,000 tokens for evidence; eight 700-token chunks use 5,600, leaving room for question and metadata. The top-k setting must obey the token budget, not just a document count.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record Evidence(String id, String revision, String text) {}
record GroundedAnswer(String text, java.util.List<String> sourceIds, boolean abstained) {}
// Reject citations absent from the authorized Evidence list.
// A citation ID must resolve to the exact revision used to answer.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

I start with a lexical/vector baseline and a small golden dataset. Add query rewriting or reranking only when observed failures justify the extra call and latency. Citation output needs evidence IDs from retrieved records rather than invented URLs.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

A top-ranked document is obsolete or includes a prompt injection. Filter by tenant, ACL and revision policy; treat source text as evidence only; preserve citations to immutable revisions so answers remain auditable.

### Security, privacy and provenance

RAG does not inherently prevent hallucination. Retrieving more chunks can increase irrelevant context and reduce answer quality.


**Verification criteria:** Measure retrieval recall, answer support, citation correctness, abstention behavior, authorization violations and freshness separately. A single similarity score cannot replace these checks.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

### Work through evaluation

Measure retrieval recall separately from answer support. If the right passage was never retrieved, changing the final prompt cannot reliably repair the missing evidence. If the passage was retrieved but the answer contradicts it, generation or context construction needs attention.

Store document, chunk and revision IDs in the answer trace. On deletion or permission change, enforce current authorization at query time and remove stale index/cached evidence under the lifecycle policy. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data, including instructions embedded in documents.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Is RAG a guarantee against hallucination?** No. Retrieval and generation can both fail.

**Does a citation ID prove support?** No. Check the cited passage actually entails the claim.

## 7. Closing answer

My RAG answer separates ingestion from query serving, retrieves only authorized current evidence, and validates the final claim-to-source relation. Missing evidence becomes an explicit answer limitation. Retrieval recall and generation support are measured separately, so failures are fixed at their actual stage.
